### The Analysis of Personality
_14th April, 1976_         p.30-p.36
It will be vague and pointless to have a discussion on the topic of personality without clinging to an appropriate definition of this particular word, so I shall attempt to define the concept of personality relative to my point of view.
When we speak of the personality of an individual, we refer to the basic and intrinsic qualities of his mental and psychological constitutions that make him unique in this world, so that, by these characteristics, one can distinguish one particular individual from others.
In the widest sense, the personality of an individual involves all the emotions, temperaments, characters and thinking methods characteristic of that particular person concerned. It must be noted that the personality of an individual is not a collective sum of static mental constitutions. It is constantly changing, evolving and transforming, being shaped by various influences, consciously or unconsciously. Yet this change of personality, in general, is subtle and gradual — to an extent it is imperceptible among the individuals concerned. Although the secondary elements in personality are changing, the primary matrices of it do not change appreciably. Unlike the personality, the character of an individual only refers to the moral constitution of a person, and does not include temperaments and emotions in general.
Under a careful scrutiny we can reduce all the mentioned processes of life — emotions, feelings, thinking methods, precepts, temperament and ideas — into a set of _a priori_ principles of life adopted by the particular individual concerned. In other words, a person applies these _a priori_ principles to any situations and problems encountered in his course of life. We may say that the personality of an individual depends on his _a priori_ principles of life, and these principles, in turn, are functions of the two main varying factors — environmental and hereditary conditions. It is important to see that these _a priori_ principles of life play a vital role in our attitudes, our conduct, our thinking methods, and our modes of life. In fact, they determine our outlook on life and our happiness. Consequently, they determine our future life, for we tend to build up our personalities through the implications and evolutions of these deep-seated principles.
Human beings have a habitual resistance to change, to reform. We tend to conform with our present social conditions and customs. We always like to follow others' path — that is, we are rather pneumatic. This proclivity of man, in fact, arises from the fear of responsibility and the fear of choice. We speak, act and think according to what is considered to be right, for many people do the same and walk the same road with us. Then we will not be alone (socially at least); hence we will feel more secure. If we do something wrong, we have the average people to fall back on, for they do the same thing, they commit the same mistake, and we are not expected to be blamed or to be punished. Rules and regulations are imposed on us to keep law and order in our society, though some of them are ridiculous and create injustice. Besides, social conventions are adopted through religions, cultures and philosophy. The children are brought up under the guidance of their parents and the teachings of  traditional social conventions adopted. These dogmatic doctrines are instilled and forced into the minds. When they grow up they will, in turn, instill their doctrines (of course, in an irrational basis) into the future generation. We always conceive ourselves to be civilized people without knowing that we are, in fact, uncivilized and raw. We do not bother to give up the war-like and brutal nature inherited by our ancestral humanoids . We like excitement and violence. Though the above observations, I would say,  the evolution of human beings, does not cope with our advancement in science and technology.
It is interesting to see that we are always frightened of dissimilarity and non-conformity — for insecure feeling rises. Every man has different faces before different groups of people; he tends to adjust his behaviours with the people he meets (I call it adaptation). Yet, the more he wants to adjust his  behaviour, the more he feels uneasy and uncomfortable. He, gradually, will lose all his confidence and remains tacit throughout.
In contrast to this fear of responsibility and failure, man is characterized by the love of power. In his limited mind he always desires to be the Infinite and to be immortal. Hence power can partly satisfy his vanity. This love of power, together with vanity, will make people compete and strive for fame. If the negative approach is taken, this will result in either crimes or dictatorship. The fear of responsibility and the love of power are two ambivalent motives in our nature.
The introduction of a supreme being and dogmas of religions and ideas have a profound impact on people. They influence our everyday life and shape our characters as well as our insight into life. Of course, they also shape our social conventions and customs adopted. Besides, the prevalent philosophical and political concepts and ideas also play a significant role in the evolution of society. As individual and society are constantly interacting with each other, these prevalent social forces (asserted by a few eminent persons) exert profound influence on individuals, thus shaping the social conventions — and these conventions, in turn, also shape the life of individuals.
The modes of education and early experiences also have a vehement impact on the personality of an individual. In general, society's dictates tend to condition individuals with the prevalent social conventions and behaviours, and — most important of all — our attitudes towards life and the world. Parents always tell their children, "You must be diligent, so that you will be well-to-do in your later life; you will live comfortably and "happily", or again, you must study, because it is for your own future." I would say that if parents teach their children in this way, they are bringing up a group of selfish, egocentric and pragmatic individuals, which may be detrimental to our society. Moreover, I would say that these concepts of life, learning and the world are dogmatic and negative. Well, it is right to say, "You must be diligent and you must study hard," but it will be completely wrong to say it is for your future well-being and comforts, for your ends — for this statement has many undesirable implications.
In the child's mind, the first concept instilled is: "Something I do must have a reward, if not,  I will not do it." The second concept: "Well-being, richness and comfort are the ONLY worthwhile goals in life, and I shall try everything to attain it." and the third concept, knowledge is only and the only means of acquiring richness and well-being. The consequence of these ideas are significant - the principles of life are built upon these assumptions: richness, comforts and well-being are the ULTIMATE goals of mankind. In order to attain these goals, money is needed. We study fort we can get a degree and earn a lot of money, so as to acquire these goals and "Take and never give"; be pragmatic, narcissistic and solipsistic. The bad effects of these principles, I think, are well exposed and need no explanation.
"Is it possible to change the personality of an individual?"
Well, to change the personality of an individual really means to change his principles of life, and hence all the deep-seated a priori assumptions of life. It is really a difficult job for one has to leave his little secure haven and accept another "insecure" (with reference to him) set of principles of life.  He may feel, for a time, that he has no reliance upon which he can trust. He may feel lost accordingly.  Another drawback is our reluctance to change.  Human beings are obstinate; they are conservatives, for it is difficult to leave something that has been relied upon. In order to overcome these problems, education and love must be furnished, so as to make him feel secure and right. (Education helps us to think rationally so that we can analyze situations and solve our problems suitably. Love can provide us with faith, security and confidence, so that we will not feel lost and insecure.)
Our future life, our happiness and our outlook, I would say, is dependent on our principles of life. Hence, it is vital for us to see that these principles of life are directed to higher ideals of life. Through our active process of learning, sublimating, and thinking, I believe that we can strive towards a goal — happiness.
